purpose:
This document sets out how {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} dispenses medications in a safe manner: dispensing is done safely by persons entitled to dispense; medication recalls are handled effectively; near-expiry medications are handled effectively at the point of dispensing; dispensed packs are labelled; high-risk medication orders are verified before dispensing; and return of medications to the pharmacy is addressed.

The chapter intent is that the organisation has a safe and organised medication process, and that dispensing is governed by written guidance. A hatch that hands over an unlabelled strip, a recalled batch that continues to leave the shelf, an expired tablet that is dispensed because the inventory list was not the act of dispensing, or a return that is poured back into a stock bottle, is not that process. This document is the dispensing process that makes the intent operational at the pharmacy and at every other location from which a medicine is issued to a patient or a clinical area.

This document is not the storage-and-inventory policy, is not the prescribing policy, and is not the administration policy. Storage, including near-expiry as inventory, is owned by the medication-storage policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.2). Prescribing is owned by the safe-and-rational-prescribing policy (MOM.3). The written order artefact is owned by the uniform-medication-orders policy (MOM.4). Administration is owned by the safe-administration policy (MOM.6). Blood units are issued under the transfusion policy (COP.5), not as dispensed medications under this labelling requirement.
scope:
This policy applies to every location at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} from which a medication is dispensed or issued: the pharmacy, a pharmacy window serving out-patients, ward or emergency issue points that operate under pharmacy oversight, and any other named dispensing location. It binds the registered pharmacist and any other person the hospital has authorised to dispense within the Pharmacy Act, 1948, the staff who receive a recall or a near-expiry alert, the staff who label a dispensed pack, the staff who verify a high-risk order before dispensing, and the staff who receive a returned medicine.

It covers: safe dispensing of medications; effective handling of medication recalls; effective handling of near-expiry medications at dispensing; labelling of dispensed medications; verification of high-risk medication orders before dispensing; and return of medications to the pharmacy.

Boundaries with other policies of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}:

- Storage of medications, including near-expiry as an inventory control (FEFO, shelf checks, quarantine of expired stock in the store), is governed by the medication-storage policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.2). This policy owns HANDLING near-expiry at the act of dispensing: a pack that is expired is not dispensed; a pack that has entered the hospital's near-expiry window is dispensed only under the written near-expiry rule at step 3, or is quarantined and not issued. MOM.2 does not decide whether yesterday's issue was expired; this document does not rewrite the store's inventory method. The two procedures must not fight: inventory finds the date; dispensing refuses the date that has passed.
- The high-risk medication LIST, including look-alike sound-alike, is defined and stored under MOM.2.c. Verification of a high-risk ORDER before dispensing is this document (MOM.5.e, Tier 2). High-risk classes of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, chemotherapeutic agents and radioactive agents — register, secure storage, preparation, administration by qualified personnel, and disposal — are governed by the high-risk-classes policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.8). This document may dispense a medicine that falls in those classes if the hospital stocks it; it hands the narcotic register, destruction and the NDPS account to MOM.8 and does not write them here.
- Blood and blood components are not "dispensed medications" under the labelling objective element of this standard. Issue, bedside identity check and transfusion are governed by the transfusion policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (COP.5). This document does not label a blood unit as a dispensed pack and does not hang a unit.
- Implantable prosthesis and medical devices are governed by the implant policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.9). They are not dispensed packs under this labelling OE.
- Returned or expired stock that becomes waste enters the hospital-wide waste programme governed by the support-services infection-control policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (HIC.3). This policy requires that such stock is not poured back into a usable bottle and is not placed in general waste; it does not restate colour categories, storage times, or common-treatment-facility handover.
- Obtaining a medicine when the pharmacy is closed is governed by the pharmacy-committee policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.1.d). This document still requires that whatever is issued in that interval is issued by a person entitled to issue it, is labelled, and is not expired.
- The written medication order is governed by the uniform-medication-orders policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.4). This policy refuses an order that is not written by an authorised person, is not legible, or lacks required content, and obtains a valid order before dispensing.
- Prepared-medication labelling at the bedside, before a second drug is prepared, is governed by the safe-administration policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.6.b). This document owns labelling of the dispensed pack. The two acts are different.
- Recalls are a hospital procedure. Powers of a licensing authority to require withdrawal from sale exist under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it. This document does not invent a national hotline, a named regulator contact, or a CDSCO telephone number as a NABH mandate.
policy_statement:
{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} dispenses medications in a safe manner. Dispensing is performed by a person entitled to dispense under the Pharmacy Act, 1948 and this hospital's written rule, against a valid order, from stock that is not expired and is not under recall.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} handles medication recalls effectively. A recalled batch is quarantined and is not dispensed.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} handles near-expiry medications effectively at dispensing. An expired medicine is not dispensed. A near-expiry pack is issued only under the written rule, or is quarantined.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} labels dispensed medications. An unlabelled pack does not leave the dispensing location.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} verifies high-risk medication orders before dispensing.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} addresses return of medications to the pharmacy. A returned pack is not restocked unless the written return rule allows it; narcotic returns are handed to the high-risk-classes policy.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} does not treat a blood unit as a dispensed medication under this document.
procedure_steps:
1. Dispensing of medications is done safely

Dispensing of medications at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is done safely. This step is the documented-evidence anchor of a requirement the standard asterisks. An assessor will ask how yesterday's issues were selected, checked and handed over, not whether a pharmacy exists. Safe dispensing is the act that stands between a written order and a pack in a patient's hand or on a ward trolley. An order that is right can still harm if the wrong pack, the wrong strength, or another patient's medicines leave the hatch.

The reason this is the safety step is that dispensing is the last systematic check before the medicine leaves professional control. Selection from a look-alike shelf, a strength that is adjacent to the intended strength, a pack handed over without matching the unique identification number, or an issue made while the dispenser is also answering a telephone, is how a correct order becomes a wrong medicine. The National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention recommendations to enhance accuracy of dispensing (chapter reference 24) describe that failure in environmental and process terms: an order should be reviewed before dispensing; the dispensing area should be designed to reduce distraction; inventory should be arranged so that similar products can be distinguished; replenishment should be checked; delivery to clinical areas should be controlled; and a standard operating procedure with a system of checks should be followed and reviewed. This document uses that Council's recommendations as a recognised framework. It does not import a named cabinet brand, a bar-code mandate, a staffing ratio, or a USP chapter as a NABH requirement. It requires that this hospital has a written dispensing method and that the method is the method used at the hatch.

Who may dispense is a person entitled to dispense under the Pharmacy Act, 1948 — typically a registered pharmacist — and any further hospital rule for a named setting. The named roles, and the rule when the pharmacist is not physically present (including the closed-pharmacy pathway owned by MOM.1.d), are [Hospital to define — who may dispense, by location, and the rule when the pharmacist is not physically present]. A person who is not entitled to dispense does not select, pack or hand over a medicine. Human-resource procedures verify pharmacist registration; this step uses that verification. This step does not restate the credentialing file.

The written dispensing method — how the order is read, how the product is selected, how the selection is checked against the order (medicine, strength, form, quantity), how the patient's name and unique identification number are matched, how an incomplete or illegible order is returned under the uniform-medication-orders policy rather than guessed, and how the pack is handed over — is [Hospital to define — the written dispensing method, including the check against the order and against the patient's name and unique identification number]. An order that is not written by an authorised person, is not legible, or lacks required content under MOM.4 is not dispensed. The common error is "the doctor meant this" followed by a pack leaving the hatch. That error is forbidden here.

Locations from which dispensing is done, and how medicines are delivered to clinical areas so that the labelled pack remains the pack that was checked, are [Hospital to define — the named dispensing locations and how labelled packs are delivered to clinical areas]. A second, unnamed cupboard from which staff help themselves is not a dispensing location under this step.

Look-alike and sound-alike arrangement of stock at the dispensing point follows the high-risk list owned by the medication-storage policy; this step requires that the person selecting can distinguish the intended product. It does not rewrite the list.

Narcotic, chemotherapy and radioactive dispensing, where those agents are stocked, is still dispensing under this step and is still labelled under step 4. The register, destruction and the statutory account are owned by the high-risk-classes policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}. This step does not write them and does not name the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act as this document's statute.

The written dispensing standard operating procedure is held at [Hospital to define — where the written dispensing standard operating procedure is held].

2. Medication recalls are handled effectively

Medication recalls are handled effectively. This step is the documented-evidence anchor of that asterisked requirement. A recall that is a circular in a file, while the recalled batch continues to leave the hatch, is not handled. Effective handling means the hospital can stop a named batch from being dispensed, can find what has already been issued, and can prevent the remainder from being used.

The reason this is a documented process rather than a telephone chain is that recalls arrive through more than one door — a manufacturer's notice, a distributor's letter, a licensing-authority direction under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it, or a hospital's own discovery that a batch is defective. Staff who "heard something" and staff who were off duty the day the letter came will dispense the batch unless the method is written, owned, and used at the hatch. The common error is a notice pinned in the pharmacy office and not converted into a quarantine of the physical stock, or a recall that is applied to the main store and forgotten in a ward cupboard. That error is how a recalled medicine reaches a patient after the hospital "knew".

How {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} receives a recall, who is authorised to declare that a recall is in force for this hospital, how in-hand stock (pharmacy and every out-of-pharmacy location under pharmacy oversight) is identified and quarantined, how already-issued packs are traced so far as the records allow, and how clinical staff are told to stop using the batch, are [Hospital to define — the medication-recall procedure: who declares a recall in force, how stock is quarantined in pharmacy and out-of-pharmacy locations, how issued packs are traced, and how clinical staff are told to stop]. A quarantined batch is not dispensed. It is not "used up because it looks fine".

This hospital's recall procedure is a hospital procedure. The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it give a licensing authority powers in respect of sale and withdrawal. This step does not invent a CDSCO hotline, a named national telephone number, or a regulator contact as a NABH mandate. The hospital names its own sources of recall information and its own internal owner.

A recalled pack that cannot be returned to the supplier, and stock that is no longer usable, enters the hospital-wide waste programme under the support-services infection-control policy. This step requires that it leaves usable stock; it does not restate waste categories.

The named owner of the recall procedure is [Hospital to define — the named owner of the medication-recall procedure]. Every dispensing location, including ward stock under pharmacy oversight, is inside that owner's reach. A location that cannot be reached by a recall is not a location that should hold stock.

3. Near-expiry medications are handled effectively at dispensing

Near-expiry medications are handled effectively. This step is the documented-evidence anchor of that asterisked requirement. It is the dispensing-time act, not the store's inventory act.

The medication-storage policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} owns near-expiry as inventory: how dates are checked on shelves, how first-expiry-first-out is run, how expired stock is removed from the store, and how documentation of those checks is kept. This step owns what happens when a pack is about to be issued. The two must not fight. Inventory that records a date is useless if the hatch issues an expired strip because "the patient is waiting". Dispensing that refuses expired stock is incomplete if the store never tells the hatch which batches are near expiry. Each procedure does its own job.

An expired medicine is not dispensed. A pack whose expiry date has passed is quarantined and is not issued, not sold, and not "given free because it is only just expired". The reason this rule is absolute is that an expired medicine is not the medicine the order named. The order named a product of known quality until the date on the pack. After that date the hospital cannot stand behind the pack as that product. The common error is the near-miss that is treated as a kindness: a strip that expires this week handed to a patient whose course will run past the date, or a ward issue of a vial that expired on the night shift because the cupboard was not the pharmacy. That kindness is a dispensing of something other than the ordered medicine.

What {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} treats as near-expiry at the point of dispensing — the window before the printed date within which a pack is flagged, whether a flagged pack may still be issued if the patient's course will finish inside the remaining dating, and how a flagged or expired pack is quarantined rather than issued — is [Hospital to define — the near-expiry window used at dispensing, whether a flagged pack may be issued if the course finishes inside remaining dating, and how flagged or expired packs are quarantined]. This document does not state a number of months or days as a NABH mandate. The hospital writes its own window. MOM.2 may use the same window for inventory; this step still requires the refusal at the hatch.

Who checks the date at the moment of dispensing is the person entitled to dispense at step 1. A date check performed only in the store, and not at issue, is not this step.

Expired and unusable near-expiry stock that cannot be returned to the supplier enters the hospital-wide waste programme under the support-services infection-control policy. This step requires that it is not restocked and not dispensed; it does not restate waste categories.

4. Dispensed medications are labelled

Dispensed medications are labelled. This step is the documented-evidence anchor of a Core requirement the standard asterisks. A pack that leaves the dispensing location without a label that ties it to this patient and this medicine is not labelled for the purpose of this standard. The manufacturer's outer carton on a bulk box is not the dispensed-pack label.

The reason labelling is the safety step at issue, not at manufacture, is that the manufacturer's label names a product, not a patient. Once a strip, bottle or bag is issued against an order, the pack must carry enough for the next person — the patient, a family member, a nurse on the next shift — to know whose it is and what it is. An unlabelled envelope of loose tablets, a syringe sent to a ward with only a handwritten strength on the barrel, or another patient's name left on a reused bag, is how the right product becomes the wrong patient's medicine. The common error is "they know what they asked for" at an out-patient window, or a ward issue that relies on the trolley position. That error is forbidden here.

What the dispensed-pack label carries is [Hospital to define — the content of the dispensed-pack label]. At a minimum this hospital's label identifies the patient (name and unique identification number), the medicine, the strength, and the route or directions as this hospital has defined them for that issue. Further legal particulars of a dispensed medicine under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it are the hospital's to match to the current text of those rules; this document does not print a section number as a mandate. A pack that does not carry the hospital's defined label does not leave the dispensing location.

This labelling is the labelling of a dispensed pack. It is not the labelling of a medication prepared at the bedside immediately before administration, which is owned by the safe-administration policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.6.b) and must be done before a second drug is prepared. A nurse drawing an injection is not dispensing under this step; a pharmacy issuing a labelled pack is not administering under MOM.6. The two labels must not be treated as substitutes.

Blood units are not labelled as dispensed medications under this step. Transfusion issue is the transfusion policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}. Implantable devices are not labelled as dispensed medications under this step; they are owned by the implant policy.

How a labelled pack is checked against the order immediately before handover is part of the dispensing method at step 1. This step owns that the label exists and is on the pack that leaves.

5. High-risk medication orders are verified before dispensing

High-risk medication orders are verified before dispensing.

The high-risk medication list, including look-alike sound-alike, is the list defined under the medication-storage policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}. This step does not rewrite that list. It requires that an order for a medicine on that list is verified before the pack is issued.

How the order is verified — who performs the verification, against which elements of the order (at least that the medicine, strength, route and frequency can be read from a valid MOM.4 order), and how a mismatch is returned to the prescriber — is [Hospital to define — how a high-risk medication order is verified before dispensing, by whom, and how a mismatch is returned]. Dispensing does not proceed on an unverified high-risk order.

Narcotic, chemotherapy and radioactive orders remain under the further rules of the high-risk-classes policy. Verification here does not replace those rules.

6. Return of medications to the pharmacy is addressed

Return of medications to the pharmacy is addressed. This step is the documented-evidence anchor of that asterisked requirement. Addressed means there is a written rule for what may come back, what happens to it, and what must never be restocked. A cardboard box under the hatch into which leftover strips are dropped without a decision is not a return process.

The reason a return rule is a safety process, not a thrift process, is that a pack that has left professional control is no longer known stock. It may have been stored in a hot car, opened, mixed with another patient's medicines, or held past expiry. Pouring it back into a stock bottle, or putting a used strip back on the shelf because the seal "looks intact", is how an uncontrolled product re-enters the dispensing chain. The common error is economy: a nearly-full bottle returned from a discharged patient restocked to avoid wastage. That economy is a contamination and an identity failure. It is forbidden unless the written rule, on defined conditions, allows a defined class of unopened return to be restocked, and those conditions are met and recorded.

What may be returned, who may accept a return, the conditions (if any) on which an unopened pack may be restocked, and the rule that an opened, unlabelled, expired, recalled, or temperature-doubtful pack is not restocked, are [Hospital to define — what may be returned to the pharmacy, who may accept a return, whether any class of unopened pack may be restocked and on what conditions, and the rule that opened, unlabelled, expired, recalled or temperature-doubtful packs are not restocked]. A pack that is not restocked is quarantined. If it is waste, it enters the hospital-wide waste programme under the support-services infection-control policy. This step requires that decision; it does not restate waste categories.

Returns of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, and any destruction or statutory register entry those returns require, are handed to the high-risk-classes policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}. This step does not write the narcotic register and does not name the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act as this document's statute. Chemotherapy and radioactive returns likewise remain under MOM.8.

Patient's-own medicines brought from outside, if they are not to be used, are not "returns to pharmacy stock". They are governed by the safe-administration policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (MOM.6.i). This step does not convert a family's bottle into hospital stock.

The written return rule is held with the dispensing standard operating procedure at step 1.

7. Records, review and the order of operations

Every dispensing episode that this document requires to be retrievable is recorded against the unique identification number where a named patient is involved: the person who dispensed, the check against the order, the label, any high-risk verification, and any refusal to dispense (expired, recalled, incomplete order, unverified high-risk order). Recalls, near-expiry quarantines and returns are recorded even when they are not tied to a single patient.

The quality or accreditation coordinator audits a sample of these records at [Hospital to define — the audit interval for dispensing, recall, near-expiry, labelling and return records] for: dispensing only by a person entitled to dispense, against a valid order, from stock that was not expired and not under recall; recalled batches quarantined rather than issued; expired packs not dispensed; dispensed packs labelled; high-risk orders verified before issue; and returns handled under the written rule rather than poured back into stock.

This policy is reviewed at [Hospital to define — the review interval for this policy], and sooner when a recalled or expired pack is found to have been issued, an unlabelled pack left the hatch, a high-risk order was issued unverified, a return was restocked against the rule, or when the storage, prescribing, order, administration, high-risk-classes, transfusion or waste policies that this document hands work to are revised.
responsibility:
The head of the institution is accountable for {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} dispensing medications only in a safe manner: by persons entitled to dispense, against valid orders, from stock that is not expired and not under recall, labelled, with high-risk orders verified, and with returns addressed.

The named pharmacist or pharmacy in-charge authors and keeps current the dispensing standard operating procedure, the recall procedure, the near-expiry-at-dispensing rule, the dispensed-pack label, the high-risk-order verification method, and the return rule. The named person is [Hospital to define — the named pharmacist or pharmacy in-charge].

Persons who dispense select, check, label and hand over only under that procedure, refuse expired, recalled, incomplete or unverified high-risk orders, and accept returns only under the return rule.

Clinical staff who hold out-of-pharmacy stock under pharmacy oversight apply recall quarantine, near-expiry refusal and labelled-pack discipline in those locations, and do not run a second unnamed dispensary.

The quality or accreditation coordinator audits the records at step 7 and reports findings to the head of the institution.

All staff are expected to treat issue of an expired or recalled pack, an unlabelled pack leaving the hatch, an unverified high-risk issue, and restocking of a pack that the return rule forbids, as defects, and to report them.
references_text:
- National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH), Standards for Small Healthcare Organisations, 3rd Edition — Chapter 3 Management of Medication, standard MOM.5 (drafted from the chapter-summary subject "Medications are dispensed in a safe manner" and the six dispensing objective elements; not from the corrupted OE-page header and not from shco_full_oes.standard_text).
- Pharmacy Act, 1948 and the rules and State pharmacy-council registration under it — insofar as they govern who may dispense medications.
- Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it — insofar as they govern labelling of dispensed medicines, sale or supply, and recall or withdrawal from sale by a licensing authority. No section number is imported as a mandate. No national hotline is invented as a NABH requirement.
- National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention, Recommendations to Enhance Accuracy of Dispensing Medications (chapter reference 24) — a recognised framework for review of the order, the dispensing environment, distinguishing similar products, replenishment checks, controlled delivery, and a standard operating procedure with a system of checks; this document does not import named cabinet brands, bar-code mandates or staffing ratios.
- Internal documents of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}: the dispensing standard operating procedure; the authorised dispensers; the medication-recall procedure; the near-expiry-at-dispensing rule; the dispensed-pack label; the high-risk-order verification method; the return rule; the medication-storage policy; the pharmacy-committee policy; the prescribing and uniform-order policies; the safe-administration policy; the high-risk-classes medication policy; the transfusion policy; the implant policy; the support-services infection-control policy; and the human resource policies.
distribution:
Controlled master copy: office of the head of the institution, {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, with the quality or accreditation coordinator.

Copies issued to: the pharmacy and every named dispensing location; every in-patient ward that holds medication stock under pharmacy oversight; the emergency area; day-care; out-patient pharmacy windows; nursing administration; and the named pharmacist or pharmacy in-charge.

The current version is available to all staff at [Hospital to define — intranet location or nursing station folder]. The dispensing standard operating procedure, the recall procedure, the near-expiry-at-dispensing rule, the dispensed-pack label content, and the return rule — the working documents this policy requires — are held at every named dispensing location.

Superseded versions are withdrawn from all points of use on issue of a revision, and one dated copy of each is retained by the quality or accreditation coordinator.
abbreviations:
Abbreviations already defined in the HIC.1 to HIC.6 master policies are not repeated here. A reader using this document on its own should refer to those policies for the shared glossary, including NABH, SHCO, OE, WHO, SOP and PPE.

The following abbreviations are used in this document and are not defined in HIC.1 to HIC.6:

NCCMERP — National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention
FEFO — First Expiry, First Out
UID — Unique Identification Number
LASA — Look-Alike Sound-Alike

Any additional abbreviation used locally within {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is [Hospital to define] and is added to this list at the next revision.
disclaimer:
This document is a template prepared for the guidance of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} and must be reviewed, adapted and formally approved by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} before use. Every entry marked [Hospital to define] must be replaced with the hospital's own decision; a document issued with those markers left in place is not an approved policy.

Several requirements in this document are statutory rather than advisory — in particular those arising under the Pharmacy Act, 1948, insofar as it governs who may dispense medications, and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it insofar as they govern labelling of dispensed medicines, sale or supply, and recall or withdrawal from sale. Statutory requirements change, and State authorities impose additional or stricter conditions. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is responsible for verifying the current text of any rule cited here and the conditions attached to its own authorisations and licences; this document does not constitute legal advice.

The clinical and technical content reflects recognised national and international guidance current at the date of preparation. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} remains responsible for verifying that it is current and consistent with the edition of the accreditation standard against which it is being assessed.

This document is not issued by, endorsed by, or affiliated with NABH, the World Health Organization, the National Centre for Disease Control, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, any Pollution Control Board, or any other body named in it. Wording is original; no text has been reproduced from the standards, rules or guidelines referenced.

oe_mapping.responsible: Named pharmacist holds the near-expiry-at-dispensing rule; persons who dispense check the date at issue and refuse expired stock; medication-storage policy owns inventory near-expiry; quality or accreditation coordinator audits

oe_mapping.evidence: The written content of the dispensed-pack label, identifying at a minimum the patient (name and unique identification number), the medicine, the strength, and the route or directions as this hospital defined them for that issue, with further legal particulars matched by the hospital to the current text of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it rather than a section number printed as a mandate; sample issues showing a pack did not leave the dispensing location without that label, and showing that a manufacturer's outer carton on a bulk box, an unlabelled envelope of loose tablets, or another patient's name on a reused bag was not treated as this label; the recorded distinction that this labelling is of a dispensed pack and is not a substitute for bedside prepared-medication labelling owned by the safe-administration policy, and that a nurse drawing an injection is not dispensing under this step; the recorded statement that blood units are not labelled as dispensed medications and remain under the transfusion policy, and that implantable devices remain under the implant policy; handover checks against the order as part of the dispensing method at step 1; the audit sample at step 7 of dispensed packs labelled
oe_mapping.responsible: Named pharmacist holds the dispensed-pack label content; persons who dispense apply the label before handover; transfusion policy owns blood-unit issue; administration policy owns bedside prepared-medication labels; quality or accreditation coordinator audits

oe_mapping.requirement: High-risk medication orders are verified before dispensing.
oe_mapping.evidence: The written method for verifying a high-risk medication order before dispensing, by whom, against a valid order, and how a mismatch is returned; the recorded use of the high-risk list defined under the medication-storage policy rather than a second list; sample high-risk issues showing verification before the pack was issued; recorded forward reference that narcotic, chemotherapy and radioactive rules remain under the high-risk-classes policy
oe_mapping.responsible: Persons who dispense verify a high-risk order before issue; medication-storage policy owns the high-risk list; high-risk-classes policy owns NDPS, chemo and radioactive rules; quality or accreditation coordinator audits

oe_mapping.requirement: Return of medications to the pharmacy is addressed.
oe_mapping.evidence: The written return rule stating what may be returned, who may accept a return, the conditions if any on which an unopened pack may be restocked, and the rule that an opened, unlabelled, expired, recalled or temperature-doubtful pack is not restocked, showing a decision process rather than a cardboard box under the hatch, and rather than a nearly-full bottle from a discharged patient poured back into a stock bottle for economy; sample returns showing restocking only where the written conditions were met and recorded, and showing packs that were not restocked quarantined and, if waste, entered into the hospital-wide waste programme under the support-services infection-control policy without colour categories restated here; the recorded handover of narcotic, psychotropic, chemotherapy and radioactive returns, and any destruction or statutory register those returns require, to the high-risk-classes policy, with the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act not treated as this document's statute; the recorded distinction that patient's-own medicines brought from outside are not returns to pharmacy stock and remain under the safe-administration policy; the written return rule held with the dispensing standard operating procedure; induction or briefing records showing staff who accept returns apply the rule rather than restocking by default; the audit sample at step 7 of returns handled under the written rule rather than poured back into stock
oe_mapping.responsible: Named pharmacist holds the return rule; persons who accept returns apply it and do not restock a pack the rule forbids; high-risk-classes policy owns narcotic return registers and destruction; administration policy owns patient's-own medicines; quality or accreditation coordinator audits

   All six objective elements on the OE page are about DISPENSING (safe dispensing; recalls; near-expiry; labelling of dispensed medications; high-risk order verification before dispensing; return to pharmacy), not prescribing.
   This draft was written from the chapter-summary subject plus those six dispensing OEs. It was NOT drafted from shco_full_oes.standard_text and NOT from the corrupted OE-page header. The policy title is "Safe Dispensing of Medications". The phrase "prescribed safely and rationally" is not used as this policy's title.
   The database field shco_full_oes.standard_text (and the matching JSON) still needs a separate data-fix pass; this draft does not fix shco_full_oes.
   Levels: MOM.5.a Commitment, MOM.5.b Commitment, MOM.5.c Commitment, MOM.5.d Core, MOM.5.e Core, MOM.5.f Commitment.
   FIVE OEs CARRY THE ASTERISK -- MOM.5.a, MOM.5.b, MOM.5.c, MOM.5.d and MOM.5.f. This is 5-of-6 asterisked, the densest Tier 1 in the chapter. The draft builds five deep blocks (steps 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6). MOM.5.e is unasterisked and is correspondingly Tier 2.
   Verified three ways on 2026-08-17: scripts/asterisk_extract.py re-run against the freshly downloaded PDF (self-validation passed; 408 OEs, 132 asterisks; output matched committed scripts/shco_oe_asterisks.json on all 408 entries), the MOM.5 page read directly from the extracted page text, and the committed asterisk file. MOM.5 was not among the 14 mismatches of the 2026-08-10 audit (the asterisks were right; the standard_text copy-paste is a different error, logged 2026-08-11).

TIERING UNDER THE STANDING RULE
1. Two-tier depth standing rule of 2026-08-10 applies. FIVE OF SIX OEs ARE TIER 1. Tier 1: MOM.5.a, b, c, d, f -- steps 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 carry the reasoning (why the hatch is the last systematic check; why a recall in a file is not a recall; why inventory near-expiry and dispensing near-expiry must not fight; why a manufacturer's carton is not a dispensed-pack label; why a return is a safety process not a thrift process). Tier 2: MOM.5.e (step 5) -- requirement and method without extended rationale. Reviewer to note the shallower treatment of e is a DECISION UNDER THE STANDING RULE, not an omission.

CROSS-REFERENCE AND OVERLAP CHECK
2. Tier 1 cross-check (2026-08-17) of MOM.5.a/b/c/d/f against the approved HIC.1-HIC.6 masters and the AAC.1-AAC.8 and COP.1-COP.13 drafts. Search terms: dispens, pharmacy, recall, expir, label, return of medication, Schedule H.
   MOM.2 -- owns storage including near-expiry as inventory. MOM.5.c owns HANDLING near-expiry at dispensing (do not dispense expired; quarantine). Split explicitly in Scope and step 3 so the two procedures do not fight.
   MOM.2.c -- high-risk LIST. MOM.5.e -- verification of high-risk ORDERS before dispensing (T2). MOM.8 -- high-risk classes NDPS/chemo/radioactive. Stated in Scope.
   COP.5 -- blood units are not "dispensed medications" under this labelling OE. Transfusion issue is COP.5. Stated in Scope and step 4.
   HIC.3 -- returned/expired waste enters the hospital-wide waste programme. Colour categories are not restated. BMW Rules are not named in P2.

   MOM.6.i -- patient's-own medicines are not pharmacy-stock returns.
   MOM.9 -- implants are not dispensed packs.

3. FORWARD REFERENCES: MOM.2 storage and high-risk list; MOM.1 closed pharmacy; MOM.3/4 order; MOM.6 administration labelling and patient's-own meds; MOM.8 NDPS register/destruction; MOM.9 implants; COP.5 transfusion; HIC.3 waste programme; HRM pharmacist registration. Each is a deliberate boundary.
4. T2 QUICK CHECK: MOM.5.e vs MOM.2.c high-risk list and MOM.8 high-risk classes -- flagged in Scope and step 5. Nothing added to the HIC reconciliation list.

STATUTORY AND EXTERNAL FACTS
5. Pharmacy Act, 1948 -- cited insofar as it governs who may dispense. No section number. Hospital-defined roles when the pharmacist is not present are additional, not a substitute for the Act. Human-resource procedures verify registration.
6. Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules under it -- cited insofar as labelling of dispensed medicines, sale or supply, and recall or withdrawal from sale. No section number. No invented CDSCO hotline.
7. NDPS Act 1985 is NOT named in P2. MOM.5 dispenses; MOM.8 owns the narcotic register and destruction. Narcotic returns are handed to MOM.8 in step 6.
8. NCCMERP Recommendations to Enhance Accuracy of Dispensing Medications (chapter ref 24, adopted 1999, revised 2015) -- verified from nccmerp.org 2026-08-17: pharmacist review of the order before dispensing; access to the profile; dispensing-area design to reduce distraction; inventory arranged to distinguish similar products; replenishment checks; controlled delivery; SOP with a system of checks; CQI on errors. Used as a framework. NOT used as a bar-code mandate, a named ADC brand, or a staffing ratio.
9. NO NUMBERS ARE STATED as requirements -- no near-expiry months, no recall-hour windows, no label-font sizes. Every such value is [Hospital to define]. Consistent with the no-numbers default.
10. Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 are NOT named in P2. Waste of returned/expired stock is pointed at HIC.3 without restating colours.

EDITORIAL POSITIONS TAKEN
11. Drafting MOM.5 as a dispensing policy titled "Safe Dispensing of Medications", against the corrupted OE-page header and against shco_full_oes.standard_text, is an editorial position required by the owner's instruction and by the 2026-08-11 data-error log. It is not a rewrite of the PDF's OE list.
12. Step 3's absolute refusal to dispense expired stock, including "only just expired" and "given free", is an editorial position; the standard requires effective handling of near-expiry, not this sentence.
13. Step 6's default that a return is not restocked unless a defined unopened class meets written conditions is an editorial position; the standard requires that return is addressed, not a ban on restocking.
14. Step 2's refusal to invent a CDSCO hotline as a NABH mandate is an editorial position required by the owner's instruction.
15. Step 4's statement that a manufacturer's carton is not the dispensed-pack label, and that blood units are not dispensed medications, are editorial positions required by the overlap instructions.
